demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I force myself to think only positive thoughts
I try to push them out of my mind

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person
I have to be on guard all the time
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Rajesh, an 80-year-old widowed South Asian man and retired Coast Guard officer, still cannot piece together the night he accidentally caused a serious injury to his crewmate. During a 1992 storm rescue off Cape May, a miscommunication led him to give an order that sent a young seaman into a crush between the rescue boat and a cargo vessel. When Rajesh tries to deliberately recall what happened, his memory offers only fragments-the distorted shout, the thud, the salt spray-that never form a coherent sequence. Yet the memory returns unbidden in full sensory reliving, triggered by the sound of a siren or the sight of the ocean. The sirens from emergency vehicles near his coastal home instantly pull him into the reliving, and the intensity of the memory makes him feel deeply unsafe, as if the danger is still present. To cope, he tells himself it did not really happen, a magical thinking that temporarily dulls the pain but also makes the memory even more fragmented and elusive when he later tries to access it. By never letting himself fully face what had happened, he never gave his brain the chance to learn that the danger was over-the threat remained as immediate and pressing as it was the night of the accident. And because the memory intruded so vividly and without warning, he began to notice that even ordinary sounds-a distant foghorn, the low hum of a fishing boat-would instantly sharpen his senses, each noise now feeling like a possible prelude to a siren.

The triggers have spread beyond sirens. Being in nature-walking along a wooded trail or sitting on a beach-immediately reinforces his belief that he is a defective person who caused harm because of his character. He has come to believe that the event happened because he is fundamentally flawed, a conviction that makes him hypervigilant: he must be on guard at all times, scanning for any sign of danger. Once he had branded himself as defective, nearly anything could confirm it-a stranger's stern glance, a dropped tool, the rumble of a boat engine-and he began to see such triggers around every corner. That hypervigilance, in turn, makes him more attuned to triggers: he notices sirens before anyone else, and even casual talk about the future from his children feels like a threat because it forces him to confront what he has made of himself. When his daughter mentions planning a family reunion next summer, the future orientation spikes his negative appraisals-he does not deserve to be part of a future-and he immediately seeks a safe seat in the corner of the room, back to the wall, to manage the overwhelming threat.

His hypervigilance and avoidance of unfamiliar places-he refuses to visit new neighborhoods because he cannot assess the danger-reinforce his sense of being defective. Each time he avoids a new place, he tells himself that a normal person would not feel this threatened, and the threat itself brings the memory rushing back: as he scans a room for exits, a flash of the rescue boat's deck appears unbidden. The feeling of threat also narrows his attention to potential dangers, making him hyper-aware of any siren or unfamiliar sound, and these triggers then loop him back into the memory and the conviction that there is something wrong with him. To cope with the defective self, he forces himself to think only positive thoughts-"I was just doing my job, it was an accident"-but this thought suppression backfires; later the memories return even more vividly, and the failure of his positive reframing deepens his negative appraisals.

In recent months, Rajesh has adopted a pattern of risky behavior that puzzles his adult children. He sometimes takes unnecessary chances-driving at high speeds along coastal roads, or walking alone through unfamiliar parks at night-as if courting danger. This risky behavior is his way of reasserting control over the threat he constantly feels, but it also increases his exposure to triggers: a sudden siren while driving sends him into a reliving episode that forces him to pull over, shaking. The magical thinking that the event never happened allows him to enter these dangerous situations, but the consequences only strengthen his negative appraisals. When he came home shaking after a walk near the harbor, he told himself again that he was a defective person who could not even manage a simple stroll. In those moments, he tries to suppress the memory by reciting a positive mantra, but the fragmented pieces break through anyway, and the cycle tightens.

The final push to seek help came two weeks ago, when he froze in a grocery store after a fire truck passed outside, and a stranger had to guide him to a seat. His eldest son, who had noticed the worsening avoidance and the risky drives, insisted he see a psychologist. Rajesh came reluctantly, terrified that talking about the future-discussing what kind of treatment might lie ahead-would only confirm that he is beyond repair. Yet underneath that fear is the faint hope that someone might help him believe that the accident does not define who he is.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory itself leads to increased sensitivity to triggers or creates new triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."

The vignette does not show that the patient's maladaptive coping strategies directly increase his sense of threat; any influence is indirect through triggers or memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the patient's negative beliefs about himself cause him to perceive or encounter triggers more frequently; instead, triggers cause negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not show that the patient's maladaptive coping strategies directly increase his sense of threat; any influence is indirect through triggers or memory.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
